Some environmentalists call for a ban on the production and utilization of plastics as the only credible way to reduce plastic waste in the environment. Given the integral role of plastics in modern society, this is an unrealistic expectation. Moreover, plastic waste can be seen as a valuable resource if recovered and remanufactured into new products. There are multiple emerging technologies that can convert plastic waste into new chemicals, fuels, and new plastics (e.g., pyrolysis) and/or the breakdown of multilayer films into their original plastic building blocks (e.g., solvent-targeted recovery and precipitation, STRAP) (Xu et al., 2020). 1.2 Solvent Based Recycling (STRAPTM) Solvent-based or dissolution based recycling is a new developing technology aiming to mechanically recycle plastics through dissolution in solvent to recover plastic with virgin like properties. The technique has been shown to be effective for polyolefins, poly vinyl chloride (PVC), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polystyrene (PS), and several others at lab or commercial scales. Solvent-based recycling is effective at separating polymer from additives and maintaining polymer value (Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2024). Research is ongoing on how to remove specific classes of contaminants ranging from pigments, plasticizers, and fillers (Arends et al., 2012; Cuthbertson et al., 2024; Wagner & Schlummer, 2024). Wisconsin partners have developed a specific technology to target multilayer plastics and complex plastics mixtures that can recover each polymer separately. From multilayer films, PE and EVOH can be separated from PET, shown in Figure 1.3. The solvent used to target each polymer is selected through guided computational calculations for polymer solubility in a given polymer. These calculations are guided with Hansen solubility parameters, molecular dynamic simulations, and conductor-like screening model for realistic solvents (COSMO-RS). Figure 1.3. Sample STRAP process to recover PE, EVOH, and PET. This particular process uses anti-solvents, but they can be replaced with cooling. Several dissolution technologies exist and mainly differ in the solvent and processing conditions used. These various conditions have been adapted to specific feedstocks such as sachet packaging waste at CreaSolv and industrial PP scraps at PureCycle (Xu et al., 2025). Many technologies in this field target feedstocks that are often landfilled as they cannot be repurposed easily. The dissolution technique aims to provide plastic circularity through conservation of the plastic’s value in the supply chain. The goal is to recycle the plastic into the same application as it was used for before recycling. Through this approach, less material can be down-cycled into lower value applications. It is important to note that not all plastic feedstocks may be suitable for economically feasible dissolution processes. This technology works best in feedstocks that have a high percent content of one polymer with other minor additives. The technique becomes more challenging in the case of a blend of various plastics with a low portion in the overall blend.
